summary: Specifies a protocol for carrying Remote Procedure Call messages over transports that support remote direct memory access. It needs no change to RPC applications or to RPC itself. It replaces RFC 5666 and is updated by RFC 8797.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers can write into each other's memory directly, which is fast. This lets remote function calls use that fast path.

questions: what is a read chunk in rpc over rdma
what is the rpc over rdma inline threshold
subtitle: How Remote Procedure Call messages ride on RDMA networks, with big data placed straight into the receiver's memory.

tldr.problem: RDMA networks move data between computers without extra copying, but they behave differently from UDP or TCP, so Remote Procedure Call (RPC) needs its own precise rules for carrying messages on them.
tldr.mechanism: Each RPC message is wrapped in an RPC-over-RDMA message with an XDR-encoded header that carries flow-control credits and lists of memory regions (chunks). Small messages travel in one RDMA Send, and bulk data is pulled or pushed with RDMA Read and Write.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 5666 and stays interoperable with it, because the protocol version number is still 1. RFC 8797 updates it.

today: RFC 8166 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2017. It obsoletes RFC 5666 and is updated by RFC 8797.

sections.title: Why RPC Needs an RDMA Binding
sections.content:
RFC 8166 specifies RPC-over-RDMA version 1, a protocol for carrying Remote Procedure Call (RPC) messages on transports that support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA). It needs no change to application RPC protocols or to RPC itself. It is based on existing implementations of RFC 5666 and obsoletes that document.

Most RPC implementations use UDP or TCP. On UDP, RPC messages sit inside datagrams. On a TCP byte stream, a record marking protocol marks where each message ends. RDMA transports differ from both: they keep message boundaries like UDP, give reliable and sequenced delivery like TCP, and add an offloaded bulk transfer service that neither provides. RPC therefore treats RDMA as a new transport type.

The Network File System (NFS) protocols are the obvious beneficiaries, but many other RPC-based protocols can also benefit. The protocol version number has not changed, because the protocol in this document fully interoperates with implementations of RFC 5666.
sections.plainLanguage: Remote function calls normally travel over slow mail-like channels. RDMA is a faster channel, so the calls need new instructions for using it.

sections.title: RPC, XDR and RDMA Building Blocks
sections.content:
The RFC builds on three pieces. An Upper-Layer Protocol (ULP) is an RPC program and version, such as NFS version 4.0. The client side of an RPC conversation is the Requester, which sends an RPC Call message. The server side is the Responder, which sends back an RPC Reply message. The Call and Reply carry the same transaction ID (XID) so they can be matched.

External Data Representation (XDR) is how RPC turns data into a byte stream without depending on endianness. Its smallest unit is four octets. If an item is not a multiple of four octets, zero octets are added after it. The RFC calls this XDR roundup.

The protocol assumes the RDMA transport offers a few abstract operations. Registered memory is a region identified by a steering tag of no more than 32 bits, with addresses of up to 64 bits. RDMA Send and Receive move messages into buffers the receiver posted in advance. RDMA Write places data directly into a remote memory region. RDMA Read pulls data from a remote region. RDMA Writes are ordered with respect to RDMA Sends but not with respect to each other.
sections.plainLanguage: One computer is the person asking, the other is the person answering. They agree on a way to write down information, and they have some special tools for dropping things directly into each other's memory.

sections.title: Credits and Inline Thresholds
sections.content:
RDMA receivers must have buffers ready before a Send arrives. If a buffer is missing or too small, the connection can be terminated, unlike TCP/IP where buffers are allocated as messages arrive. So each connection has two limits.

The first is the credit, the capability to handle one RPC-over-RDMA transaction. Each message from Requester to Responder requests a number of credits, and each message back says how many were granted, in the rdma_credit field. A Requester MUST NOT send unacknowledged requests beyond the granted limit, and the granted value MUST NOT be zero, because that would deadlock the connection.

The second is the inline threshold, the largest message that fits in one RDMA Send and Receive. Each connection has a call inline threshold and a reply inline threshold. These are not advertised in the protocol. At connection start, peers can rely on one RPC at a time with Call and Reply messages of no more than 1024 bytes. Receivers MUST support inline thresholds of 1024 bytes, and senders MUST assume 1024 bytes unless another mechanism says otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a restaurant with a limited number of tables and a limited plate size. You can only send as many orders as tables the kitchen says are free, and each order must fit on the plate.

sections.title: Chunks and Direct Data Placement
sections.content:
To avoid copying large data, a sender can remove an item from the message and move it separately. The removed piece is a chunk, and a message with chunks taken out is called reduced. The message always has two XDR streams: the Transport stream (the RPC-over-RDMA header) and the Payload stream (the RPC message itself, beginning with its XID).

Only items marked DDP-eligible in an Upper-Layer Binding (ULB) specification may be reduced. A ULB is an extra document that says which XDR items of a ULP may use direct data placement. Each RPC program and version that uses this protocol needs one. Senders MUST NOT reduce items that are not DDP-eligible.

A chunk is made of RDMA segments, each with a handle, a length and an offset. A Read chunk holds data the Responder pulls from the Requester, and each of its read segments also carries a Position field saying where the data is reinserted in the Payload stream. A Write chunk is an array of segments the Responder fills by pushing data to the Requester. Because the Requester must size a Write chunk before the reply exists, it MUST register chunks long enough for the largest possible result.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of stuffing a huge package into an envelope, you put a note in the envelope saying exactly where the package is. The other side then fetches it, or drops its answer in a spot you marked.

sections.title: Short, Chunked and Long Messages
sections.content:
The RFC describes three ways to send a message, depending on its size. A short message is smaller than the inline threshold, so the Payload stream is simply appended to the Transport stream in one RDMA Send. The RFC notes that an NFS version 3 GETATTR call is only 56 bytes.

A chunked message has DDP-eligible items removed. The header and reduced payload go in one RDMA Send. The Responder then uses RDMA Read to fetch argument data from Read chunks, and uses RDMA Write to push result data into Write chunks before sending the reply.

A long message is used when the payload is still too big after reduction. The sender conveys only the Transport stream in the Send, and the Payload stream moves by RDMA. A Long Call uses a Position Zero Read chunk, where every read segment has Position zero. A Long Reply uses a single Reply chunk that the Requester provides in advance. A Requester MUST provide a Reply chunk whenever the largest possible reply could exceed the reply inline threshold.
sections.plainLanguage: A short note goes in the envelope. A note with an attachment points to where the attachment is. A very long letter is left on a table, and the envelope only says where to find it.

sections.title: The RPC-over-RDMA Header
sections.content:
Every header is XDR encoded and starts with four fixed 32-bit fields: rdma_xid, rdma_vers, rdma_credit and the procedure number rdma_proc. These four MUST keep the same meanings and positions in all later versions. The XID MUST match the XID in the RPC message, and the version for this protocol MUST be one (1).

The procedure number tells what follows. RDMA_MSG (0) means chunk lists and a Payload stream follow. RDMA_NOMSG (1) means there is no Payload stream, and one of the chunk lists must hold it. RDMA_ERROR (4) reports a header encoding error. RDMA_MSGP (2) and RDMA_DONE (3) are reserved and not to be used.

After the fixed fields come three optional-data items: the Read list, the Write list and the Reply chunk. Each may be marked not present. Responders MUST leave the Read list empty in all replies. Any change to the header XDR requires a new protocol version number, and new capabilities in version 1 can only come from conventions that reuse the existing XDR, described in a Standards Track RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts with a little label with four boxes: which question this is, which rule book is used, how many questions can be in flight, and what kind of message it is.

sections.title: Handling Errors
sections.content:
A receiver checks the header before passing a message up. A message shorter than the minimal header of 28 bytes MUST be silently discarded, because its XID cannot be trusted. If a Responder finds other header errors in a Call, it MUST send an RDMA_ERROR message. A Requester MUST silently discard a bad Reply, and a Responder MUST silently discard an RDMA_ERROR it receives.

Two error codes exist. ERR_VERS (1) reports an unsupported version and gives the lowest and highest versions the Responder supports. ERR_CHUNK (2) reports an XDR parsing problem, such as an invalid rdma_proc value, or a RDMA_NOMSG message with no chunk lists present. An RDMA_ERROR indicates a permanent error and completes the transaction for that XID.

RDMA operational errors, such as using a chunk whose memory is no longer registered, are typically fatal to the connection. If a Responder cannot send a reply, it MUST close the connection to tell the Requester the reply was lost. A Requester that cannot invalidate a memory region after a reply MUST close the connection to protect that memory.
sections.plainLanguage: If a letter is garbled, the receiver sends back a note saying what was wrong. If it is too garbled to even tell who sent it, the receiver just throws it away.

sections.title: Memory and Message Security
sections.content:
The main concern is protecting local memory. Use of this transport MUST NOT introduce vulnerabilities to system memory, and any RDMA provider used MUST conform to RFC 5042. Requesters should register memory for remote access only when it is about to be the target of an RDMA Read or Write, and should invalidate it as soon as the RPC finishes, including when an RPC is cancelled. Unpredictable memory handles are recommended, and persistently registered memory should not be advertised.

Denial of service is possible too. A Responder need not pull unreasonably large Read chunks. Exceeding the credit grant repeatedly can cause a self denial of service, and a Requester that keeps starting and aborting RPCs can cause repeated connection loss that hurts other users of the connection.

RPCSEC_GSS can provide authentication, integrity and privacy above this transport. If integrity or privacy is in use, a sender MUST NOT reduce a Payload stream, so no data item is DDP-eligible and the transport behaves like one without direct data placement. The Transport stream itself is not protected by RPCSEC_GSS, so protection at lower layers, such as IPsec that can be co-located in RDMA hardware, may be more suitable where performance matters.
sections.plainLanguage: If you let someone reach into your filing cabinet, you only open the drawer they need and lock it right after. And you check who they are first.

fields.name: rdma_xid
fields.desc: Transaction ID, the same as in the RPC message.

fields.name: rdma_vers
fields.desc: Protocol version; one for this protocol.

fields.name: rdma_credit
fields.desc: Credits requested in a Call or granted in a Reply.

fields.name: rdma_proc
fields.desc: Procedure number that says what follows.

items.label: RDMA_MSG
items.desc: Chunk lists and a Payload stream follow.

items.label: RDMA_NOMSG
items.desc: No Payload stream; a chunk list carries it.

items.label: RDMA_ERROR
items.desc: Signals an encoding error in the header.
